barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: A barber just finished a tight fade. Clipper blades and metal guards touched the client's scalp. What must happen before the next cut?

options.a: Clean debris off, then disinfect nonporous tools for the full EPA contact time
options.b: Spray disinfectant over hair still packed in the blades, then start the next fade
options.c: Park the clippers in a UV cabinet for two minutes and count that as disinfection
options.d: Skip disinfection unless blood was seen; brush the blades and reuse them

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Sanitation is cleaning (remove hair and soil); disinfection is the EPA-registered chemical kill step on a clean, nonporous surface. Boards expect both between clients for implements that contacted skin or hair. UV storage and spraying over debris do not replace label contact time.

distractorExplanations.b: Disinfectant cannot reach microbes through packed hair; cleaning must come before the EPA contact time.
distractorExplanations.c: UV cabinets store already-disinfected tools; they are not an EPA hospital-disinfectant step.
distractorExplanations.d: Multi-use tools that touched skin or hair are cleaned and disinfected every client, not only after blood.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: During a straight-razor shave, the barber nicks the client's neck and blood appears. What is the correct next sequence?

options.a: Finish the remaining passes first, then put antiseptic on the nick
options.b: Stop, glove, apply antiseptic, and discard blood-soiled single-use items
options.c: Press a shared styptic pencil on the nick and keep the pencil for later clients
options.d: Wipe the blood with the client's towel and continue the shave bare-handed

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: A blood exposure is a stop event under typical NIC/state infection-control outlines and OSHA bloodborne practice: gloves, antiseptic on the wound, discard contaminated porous/single-use items, then clean and disinfect nonporous tools before returning to service.

distractorExplanations.a: Finishing the shave first spreads blood and delays control; the service stops at the nick.
distractorExplanations.c: Shared styptic pencils are not permitted; styptic is single-use powder, liquid, or spray.
distractorExplanations.d: Wiping with a towel and working ungloved ignores PPE and contaminates linen that must be contained.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: A jar of EPA-registered hospital disinfectant sits at the station. After which step, and on which items, is it used?

options.a: On porous neck strips and cotton that will be reused after a soak
options.b: On shears still coated with hair, to skip a separate wash
options.c: On cleaned, nonporous implements that can withstand immersion
options.d: As a leave-on antiseptic painted on the client's face before a shave

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Hospital-level EPA disinfectant is for hard, nonporous implements after they are washed free of hair and debris. Porous single-use items are discarded. Skin is prepped with antiseptic, not immersion disinfectant. Cleaning and disinfection are sequential, not interchangeable.

distractorExplanations.a: Porous single-use items cannot be reliably disinfected; neck strips and cotton are discarded.
distractorExplanations.b: Soil blocks the chemical; hair-coated shears must be cleaned before any EPA soak.
distractorExplanations.d: EPA hospital disinfectant is not a leave-on skin product; antiseptic is used on skin.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: The barber places a paper neck strip under the cape for a new client. After the haircut, what happens to that strip?

options.a: Soak it in hospital disinfectant and reuse it for the rest of the day
options.b: Shake it off and share it if no hair or product is visible
options.c: Wash it in the shampoo bowl and hang it with the towels
options.d: Discard it as a single-use porous item; do not disinfect and reuse

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: NIC theory treats neck strips and similar porous barriers as single-use. Disinfectant does not make paper or cotton multi-use. Multi-use nonporous tools are cleaned and disinfected; porous client-contact items go in the trash after one person.

distractorExplanations.a: Hospital disinfectant is for nonporous tools; soaking a neck strip does not make it reusable.
distractorExplanations.b: Visible cleanliness is not a disinfection test; a used porous strip is never shared.
distractorExplanations.c: Shampoo-bowl washing is for hair, not a method that converts single-use paper into linen.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: After a fade, the barber brushes hair from the clipper blades and sprays an EPA clipper disinfectant. When may the blades go back into service?

options.a: After they stay wet for the full contact time printed on the product label
options.b: As soon as the spray mist looks dry, even if that is only a few seconds
options.c: After a coat of blade oil, because oil is treated as a disinfectant
options.d: After two minutes in a UV storage cabinet, which replaces the wet contact time

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: EPA clipper sprays and hospital disinfectants kill only when the surface stays wet for the listed contact time after debris is removed. Dry-to-the-touch is not the endpoint. Blade oil lubricates; UV cabinets store clean tools. Clippers are multi-use and must complete that wet step between clients.

distractorExplanations.b: Mist drying in seconds usually undercuts the label minutes required for hospital-level kill.
distractorExplanations.c: Clipper oil is lubrication, not an EPA-registered disinfectant for blades.
distractorExplanations.d: UV storage does not replace wet contact time on an EPA-registered clipper disinfectant.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: A walk-in asks for a bald fade. The barber sees open, weeping sores on the scalp. What should the barber do?

options.a: Cut over the sores while wearing gloves so the shop is protected
options.b: Decline the cut over broken skin and refer the client out
options.c: Paint antiseptic on the sores and then proceed with the clippers
options.d: Have the client sign a waiver and complete the fade as booked

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Broken, infected, or weeping skin is outside a routine barber service. Referral protects the client and the shop; gloves and antiseptic do not turn an open lesion into a safe cutting surface. Waivers do not override infection-control rules on servicing inflamed or broken scalp.

distractorExplanations.a: Gloves protect the barber but do not make cutting over open sores an allowed service.
distractorExplanations.c: Antiseptic on lesions is not a license to clip over broken skin; the client is referred out.
distractorExplanations.d: A liability waiver does not authorize servicing open scalp sores against board sanitation rules.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: Between a chemical relaxer and the next client's haircut, when must the barber wash with soap and water?

options.a: Only if that last service produced visible blood on the gloves
options.b: Once at clock-in and once at clock-out; sanitizer covers the rest
options.c: Before each service and after any blood or chemical contact
options.d: Before the next cut, using alcohol gel instead of washing after chemicals

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Handwashing is a separate control from tool disinfection. Typical shop and OSHA-aligned practice is soap and water before each client and after blood, body-fluid, or chemical exposure. Alcohol gel does not remove relaxer residue the way a wash does.

distractorExplanations.a: Hands are washed before every service, not only after visible blood.
distractorExplanations.b: Shift-only washing leaves every mid-day client without a required hand-hygiene step.
distractorExplanations.d: Hand sanitizer does not replace soap-and-water after chemical contact on the skin.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: Hot-towel shaves produce a pile of damp linens. Why does the shop keep a covered soiled-linen hamper at the station?

options.a: So a towel can be wrung out and used on a second client
options.b: So capes can stay unwashed if they only caught hair
options.c: So used neck strips can dry in the hamper and return to the drawer
options.d: So used towels are contained, not piled uncovered on the station

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Used towels are multi-use only after proper laundry, not after sitting on the station. A covered hamper keeps soiled linen contained, limits contamination of clean tools, and is the sanitation control between the shave and the wash cycle. Capes still need cleaning per shop rules; neck strips are discarded.

distractorExplanations.a: A used towel is not wrung and reused; it goes to laundry after one client.
distractorExplanations.b: The hamper does not excuse unwashed capes; hair-soiled capes are still cleaned.
distractorExplanations.c: Neck strips are single-use trash, not items dried in the linen hamper for reuse.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: Metal combs are soaking in a fresh EPA hospital-grade quat. What determines when they may be removed, rinsed, and stored?

options.a: Full label contact time on a comb that was already cleaned of debris
options.b: One minute of soak time, even with hair still in the teeth
options.c: When the solution has air-dried on the comb, ignoring listed minutes
options.d: Half the listed time because the jar was mixed this morning

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Quaternary ammonium and other EPA hospital disinfectants require pre-cleaning plus the wet contact time on the label (often several minutes, product-specific). Fresh mix does not shorten that time. Air-dry or a shop 'one minute' rule is not a substitute for the EPA directions.

distractorExplanations.b: Hair in the teeth blocks contact, and one minute is not a universal EPA contact time.
distractorExplanations.c: The surface must stay wet for the listed time; drying early can end the kill step too soon.
distractorExplanations.d: A morning mix still needs the full labeled minutes; freshness is not a time discount.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: After a shave, the barber wants to strop the straight razor. The blade still has soap and skin debris on it. What is true of the leather strop?

options.a: Stropping the soiled blade counts as disinfection because friction kills microbes
options.b: The strop is kept clean and does not replace EPA disinfection of a soiled blade
options.c: The leather should be immersed in the wet sanitizer jar like a metal comb
options.d: The strop is discarded after each client the same way as a neck strip

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: A leather strop is porous and used on a clean, already-disinfected (or unused) blade to align the edge. Stropping is not sanitation, disinfection, or sterilization. Soiled razors are cleaned and given an EPA hospital-disinfectant step (or approved sterilization) before they meet the strop.

distractorExplanations.a: Friction on leather does not equal an EPA-registered disinfection step on a dirty blade.
distractorExplanations.c: Leather is porous and is not soaked in wet sanitizer the way a metal comb is.
distractorExplanations.d: A strop is a reusable shop tool kept clean, not a single-use neck-strip equivalent.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: Hair from the last fade is still on the shop floor around the chair. What is the sanitation step before seating the next client?

options.a: Leave it until the morning sweep so traffic is not interrupted
options.b: Spray hospital disinfectant over the loose hair, then cut
options.c: Sweep the hair up so it is not tracked into the next service
options.d: Kick the hair into a corner pile and empty it at closing

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Shop sanitation includes removing hair after each service so it is not tracked onto clean linens, tools, or the next client's skin. Disinfectant sprayed over soil does not work. A single morning sweep or a closing-time corner pile leaves contamination in the work area all day.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for a morning-only sweep leaves every later client's hair on the floor.
distractorExplanations.b: Cleaning comes first; spraying EPA product over loose hair does not disinfect the floor.
distractorExplanations.d: A corner pile until close still tracks hair through the shop between clients.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: A shop owns an autoclave. How does sterilization fit with cleaning and disinfection for barber tools?

options.a: Skip washing because steam heat is enough to destroy soil and microbes
options.b: Autoclave plastic combs and nylon brushes instead of using disinfectant solution
options.c: Load towels and capes into the autoclave between clients instead of laundering
options.d: Clean heat-safe metal tools first, then autoclave if the shop uses that method

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Cleaning removes soil; disinfection reduces pathogens on nonporous tools with EPA product; sterilization (autoclave steam) destroys all microbial life on heat-safe metal after cleaning. Most shops disinfect rather than sterilize, but an autoclave never skips the wash or replaces laundry for linens.

distractorExplanations.a: Debris shields microbes from steam; pre-cleaning is still required before sterilization.
distractorExplanations.b: Most plastic combs and nylon brushes cannot take autoclave heat; they are cleaned and disinfected.
distractorExplanations.c: Towels and capes are laundered; they are not autoclave loads between haircuts.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: The immersion jar looks cloudy and the mix date is past the manufacturer's use-by window. What should the barber do?

options.a: Dump it and remix to the label; do not guess remaining strength
options.b: Pour in extra concentrate until the cloudiness clears
options.c: Keep using it through the last appointment, then dump it at close
options.d: Use the cloudy mix only as a pre-clean wash, not as disinfectant

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Cloudy, contaminated, or expired EPA hospital disinfectant is not a known concentration. Boards and labels require dumping and remixing to directions. Topping up or stretching it through the day leaves tools that look 'disinfected' without a valid kill step. Pre-cleaning uses soap and water, not spent disinfectant.

distractorExplanations.b: Adding concentrate to spent solution yields an unknown dilution and keeps the contamination.
distractorExplanations.c: Cloudy or expired solution is changed immediately, not after the last booked client.
distractorExplanations.d: Spent disinfectant is discarded; pre-cleaning is soap and water, not old hospital solution.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: The barber has weeping dermatitis on both palms at the start of the shift. What is the infection-control action?

options.a: Work faster so the remaining book finishes before the skin worsens
options.b: Pause services until the board glove or clearance rule is met
options.c: Dust extra talc on the palms and continue cutting uncovered
options.d: Hand the clipper to the client for the sides and only do the top

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: Weeping or infected skin on the barber's hands is an infection-control stop. Many boards require staying off services or using required barriers only after the condition is controlled. Speed, powder, or handing tools to the client does not isolate exudate from the next scalp.

distractorExplanations.a: Finishing the book faster still contacts every client with weeping skin.
distractorExplanations.c: Talc hides moisture; it is not PPE and does not meet a board clearance rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Letting the client run the clipper does not keep the barber's open skin off the service.

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.prompt: A regular client mentions living with hepatitis B. No blood is visible yet. How should the barber handle clippers, towels, and a later nick?

options.a: Refuse all future haircuts because HBV cannot be managed with shop protocol
options.b: Use a milder disinfectant on this client so the metal tools last longer
options.c: Apply the same EPA disinfection and blood-exposure steps used for every client
options.d: Write the diagnosis on the ticket so the shop can isolate only this person's tools

barber-state-readiness-check-infection-0.explanation: HBV and HIV shop protocol follows OSHA-style standard (universal) precautions: treat every client's blood and implements the same way—clean then EPA-disinfect multi-use tools, discard single-use, and run the nick protocol if blood appears. You do not need a posted diagnosis, and you do not weaken the disinfectant for 'low-risk' visits.

distractorExplanations.a: Known HBV is managed with the same disinfection and exposure protocol, not a blanket refusal of all cuts.
distractorExplanations.b: Milder mix undercuts hospital-level EPA kill; tool life is not a reason to dilute.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard precautions mean you do not single out a diagnosis; every client's tools get the full protocol.
